W7222954764.abstract: Breast cancer continues to be one of the leading causes of cancer-related death among women worldwide, and early detection together with timely clinical intervention remains essential for improving survival outcomes. Deep learning and Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive results in breast cancer diagnosis and medical decision support, yet their use in real clinical settings is still held back by black-box decision making, hallucinated outputs, reasoning that is not grounded in evidence, poor integration of heterogeneous patient data, and limited explainability. Most existing computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) systems focus mainly on image classification and offer little in the way of transparent clinical justification or personalized treatment guidance, which in turn undermines clinician trust and everyday usefulness. This paper proposes AgentBreast-RAG, an Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Explainable Large Language Model (ARX-LLM) framework built for breast cancer diagnosis and clinical decision support. The framework brings together multimodal patient data, mammography, ultrasound and histopathological imaging, clinical records, laboratory findings, biomarker profiles, and patient history, within a single diagnostic pipeline that is coordinated by a collaborative multi-agent ecosystem. Within this ecosystem, specialized agents handle patient profiling, medical image interpretation, evidence retrieval, clinical reasoning, explanation generation, treatment recommendation, and decision verification. An Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Agentic RAG) module retrieves and verifies medical evidence from PubMed, NCCN guidelines, ASCO recommendations, WHO resources, and peer-reviewed oncology literature in a dynamic, ongoing manner, which substantially cuts down hallucination compared to standalone LLMs. A dedicated Explainable AI (XAI) module then brings all of this together through Grad-CAM and attention visualization for imaging, SHAP-based feature attribution for structured variables, natural-language rationales grounded in the retrieved evidence, and an uncertainty estimation module that assigns confidence scores to the model's outputs. We also lay out an evaluation protocol built around seven public multimodal breast cancer resources (CBIS-DDSM, INbreast, BUSI, BreakHis, BACH, the Wisconsin Breast Cancer Dataset, and TCGA-BRCA), benchmarked against convolutional neural networks, Vision Transformers, conventional RAG, GraphRAG, and existing medical LLMs. This evaluation draws on diagnostic metrics (Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score, Specificity, Sensitivity, AUC), retrieval metrics (Recall@K, Precision@K, nDCG), and explainability metrics (faithfulness, localization accuracy, clinician interpretability rating, hallucination rate). The performance figures reported here are illustrative and clearly labeled as simulated projections rather than results from executed experiments; they are meant only to show the intended structure of the evaluation. Even so, the direction we propose suggests that combining autonomous multi-agent collaboration, verified retrieval, multimodal fusion, and interpretable decision support could meaningfully improve diagnostic reliability, evidence-grounded reasoning, and clinician confidence, pointing toward a scalable path for trustworthy, explainable AI-assisted breast cancer care.

W7222973266.abstract: States already use private actors to create distance between public authority and hostile cyber operations. Artificial intelligence does not invent that arrangement; it allows the decisive human choices to be divided again. A government may pay a private military and security company to achieve an objective. A PMSC officer may commission a developer. Developers in several States may produce separate planning, discovery, persistence, routing and reporting modules. An open-weight model may run upon privately rented or compromised infrastructure. The human supplies the objective, money and permissions, whilst the system selects targets, techniques, timing and jurisdictional route. When harm follows, every participant can describe his act as only preparatory and every territorial State can see only a fragment. This paper rejects two comfortable mistakes. The first is that autonomous offensive cyber systems belong to an indeterminate future. Public evaluations now demonstrate that agentic systems can reproduce known vulnerabilities, operate across realistic networks, coordinate multi-step tasks and, in reported misuse, perform substantial portions of espionage campaigns. Performance remains brittle, supervision remains material and benchmarks do not prove an unconstrained machine capable of attacking anything; none of those limitations makes the present capability imaginary. Older water, health, insurance and local-government systems need not present frontier problems before automation multiplies harm. The second mistake is that responsibility disappears where the machine chooses the intermediate means. A State, company or individual may remain responsible for authorising a dangerous objective, deploying a system, supplying indispensable infrastructure, failing to impose available constraints, adopting the operation, aiding another actor or deliberately designing evidential fragmentation. The paper explains six conceivable architectures without supplying operational instructions: a single objective-driven agent; a planner–executor–verifier system; a compartmentalised multi-agent system; a PMSC supply-chain system; a distributed event-driven system; and a persistence-and-recovery system capable of continuing despite node loss. It then subjects each to the law of State responsibility, the law on the use of force, international humanitarian law, international criminal law, corporate and individual criminal responsibility, procurement and due diligence. The principal conclusion is that autonomy should be treated as an allocation of decision authority, not as a mystical new actor. The law should require attribution manifests recording who set the objective, selected constraints, supplied tools and compute, approved deployment, could suspend operation and received its product. A rebuttable presumption should arise where a State or PMSC intentionally obscures those facts, and responsibility should attach to the deployment of a prohibited-risk system even where no human selected the final target. The autonomous third party is dangerous not because no person exists behind it, but because many persons can arrange matters so that no one court sees enough of them at once. Publication edition, revised October 2026; not yet peer reviewed.

W7223051296.abstract: Synthesizing a monocular video from a new camera trajectory requires preserving the observed scene geometry and motion while completing regions that become newly visible. Feed-forward 4D reconstructors recover the structure of the observed scene, whereas video diffusion models provide a generative prior for completing unseen content. We introduce Holo4D, a video reshooting framework that uses reconstructed 3D trajectories as a holistic source-view 4D scaffold. We project these trajectories into the requested views and encode their geometry and source appearance to guide a pretrained video diffusion model. Together with the source video and target cameras, the scaffold grounds generation in reconstructed observations while leaving unsupported regions to the generative prior. Experiments demonstrate the value of trajectory-based conditioning for camera control and novel-view synthesis. The framework accommodates different 4D reconstructors without retraining the video generator, allowing it to benefit from future advances in source reconstruction. More details can be found in our project page.

W7223122895.abstract: The state-space explosion problem severely limits the application of formal verification in large-scale industrial maintenance and production systems. This work introduces a novel trace-driven verification algorithm and a bounded-bottleneck detection methodology that enable interactive verification and anomaly diagnosis of industrial-scale high-level Petri net (HLPN) models, serving as a simulation-based framework for maintenance modeling. To translate these formal mathematical models into practical engineering decision support, we implement these methodologies within a multi-agent simulation architecture based on coordinated software agents. A central manager coordinates specialized tool agents that autonomously detect threshold-based bottlenecks, operational livelocks, and system deadlocks via natural language queries. The framework was validated across three use cases representing realistic industrial maintenance processes, ranging from a baseline loop to a full-scale simulation of a preventive maintenance irradiation facility. Simulation results demonstrate that while lightweight local AI inference models exhibit instability during function calling, advanced large-scale Large Language Model (LLM) architectures maintain consistent diagnostic performance in extensive industrial verification contexts. The proposed framework demonstrates how formal modeling and simulation methods can be operationalized as an integrated technology layer for scalable decision support in complex production systems. The study concludes that human-in-the-loop agentic workflows remain essential for ensuring safe and reliable maintenance decision-making in safety-critical industrial environments.

W7223300893.abstract: ABSTRACT This critical review traces the evolution of machine learning (ML) across the full value chain of heterogeneous catalysis over 2017–2026, from catalyst discovery to reactor and process design, and across the principal reaction families (CO 2 reduction, water splitting, nitrogen chemistry, zeolite‐catalyzed transformations). Each stage is evaluated against four criteria — data foundation, method maturity, experimental validation and deployment readiness — through a structured capability scorecard. Digitalization has advanced from the top of the length scale downward: prediction of adsorption energies and atomistic potential‐energy surfaces is now mature, with errors of tens of meV relative to the reference DFT calculations and accelerations of three orders of magnitude over DFT, yet experimentally validated catalyst improvements remain rare. The most significant advance is the closed‐loop autonomous laboratory coupling Bayesian optimization, automated synthesis and high‐throughput testing. Large language models have begun to add a reasoning and orchestration layer, while kinetics, reactor and process design remain the least digitalized stages. We argue that the field's next decade of impact will be decided not by more accurate atomic‐scale prediction but by carrying ML into experimental validation and the reactor‐and‐process scale, where catalysis is hardest to industrialize and where data‐driven methods are weakest.

W7223373529.abstract: Abstract Complicated urinary tract infection associated with urinary stone disease remains clinically challenging because obstruction, infected stones, delayed microbiological confirmation, and antimicrobial resistance may converge in the same patient. Artificial intelligence can support this pathway when it is framed as clinical risk integration rather than isolated image recognition. We conducted a structured narrative search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar from database inception to 31 July 2026, supplemented by reference chaining and relevant clinical and reporting guidelines. The synthesis distinguishes direct evidence in stone-associated infection and perioperative infectious outcomes from indirect evidence in stone detection, volumetry, recurrence, and general UTI stewardship. Radiomics and machine learning studies show promising discrimination, but the evidence remains predominantly retrospective and frequently lacks external validation, complete calibration reporting, and prospective impact assessment. Artificial intelligence should therefore be treated as an adjunct to urological assessment, cultures, imaging, antimicrobial stewardship, and timely source control. For African settings, pragmatic validation must account for local resistance patterns, uneven access to CT and microbiology, referral delays, infrastructure, and the availability of urgent drainage.

W7223408867.abstract: Photometric Type Ia supernova (SN Ia) cosmology in the era of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) demands statistical frameworks that simultaneously account for selection effects, photometric redshift uncertainties and non-Ia contamination at scale. We present FlowSN2, a modular statistical framework combining hierarchical Bayesian modelling and simulation-based inference (SBI), that reframes photometric SN cosmology from a regression task to a joint inference problem over light curve summaries and photometric redshifts. By employing neural likelihood estimation via normalising flows, FlowSN2 approximates the data distributions of selected objects in a form that can be reused across different cosmological models, achieving amortisation over the Hubble diagram. This amortisation enables inference across alternative cosmological parameterisations, such as $w_0w_a\mathrm{CDM}$, away from the fiducial training cosmology. The framework integrates a standardisation model that disentangles intrinsic SN variations from extrinsic host-galaxy dust effects and adopts a principled Bayesian resampling approach to propagate SN classification uncertainty, without requiring an explicit contaminant likelihood. Across simulated tests spanning five cosmological parameter sets, our framework recovers true cosmological and population parameters, with posteriors in close agreement with both tractable analytical solutions and pure-Ia baselines. Conveniently, the framework enables Bayesian model comparison at negligible additional computational cost, providing a valuable tool for addressing debates surrounding SN standardisation and evolving dark energy. Capable of scaling to over a hundred thousand SNe without retraining, FlowSN2 offers an interpretable and statistically principled solution for cosmological inference with upcoming wide-field photometric surveys.

W7223690396.abstract: Resistance of antimicrobial pathogens, such as Escherichia coli, that cause foodborne disease is becoming a major threat to One Health and food safety.In this exploratory study, we investigated whether an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted, metadata-based epidemiological inference framework could demonstrate agreement with phenotypic antimicrobial resistance profiles obtained by standard susceptibility testing.This cross-sectional agreement study evaluated the diagnostic performance of the methodology using a dataset of 132 confirmed E. coli isolates collected from food chain sources.Phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed using the Kirby-Bauer disk-diffusion technique with amoxicillin-clavulanate, ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin, and imipenem.The inference engine, based on a large language model, classified isolates based solely on contextual metadata.Resistance to multiple drugs was observed in 37.1% of samples.Phenotypic resistance was highest with amoxicillin-clavulanate (47.0%) and lowest with imipenem (6.1%).The AIassisted epidemiological inference framework demonstrated substantial agreement with the phenotypic susceptibility profiles, achieving a sensitivity of 76.9%, specificity of 86.3%, and Cohen's Kappa of 0.61.Discrepancies were higher for imipenem, which may have been due to class imbalance.Overall, there was moderate concordance between the AI-assisted inference model and the phenotypic resistance pattern in surveillance.These findings may support the development of resistance risk-stratification strategies and help prioritize confirmatory testing; however, in vitro antimicrobial susceptibility testing remains essential.

W7223780851.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is an aggressive primary brain tumor with marked molecular and cellular heterogeneity, and current treatment provides limited long-term disease control. Single-target therapies have frequently failed because tumor subpopulations can differ in signaling dependencies, adapt under treatment pressure, and interact with a complex microenvironment. This review examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can integrate multi-omics data to improve drug-target prediction in GBM. It summarizes the pathological and molecular basis of GBM, evaluates current therapeutic targets and their limitations, and compares genomic, transcriptomic, single-cell, spatial, proteomic, metabolomic, and imaging data used for target discovery. Machine-learning, deep-learning, and network-based approaches are discussed with examples of multimodal risk stratification and candidate-target identification. The review also evaluates CRISPR screening as a functional validation step that can distinguish statistical associations from genuine tumor dependencies. Overall, AI-integrated multi-omics can provide a more context-specific approach to target prioritization by linking candidate genes to patient subgroups, cell states, and pathway activity. However, small cohorts, missing data, batch effects, limited model generalizability, and insufficient experimental validation remain major barriers. Future studies should combine larger multi-centre datasets with longitudinal and spatial profiling, interpretable models, functional perturbation, and prospective validation to support clinically translatable precision therapy in GBM.

W7223814242.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents work in scenarios with very different memory needs. A question about past conversations needs the exact facts it names, while a multi-step task needs a trace of the steps already taken together with details that the next step cannot name. Existing memories are each designed and tested for one kind of scenario. Retrieval memories such as A-Mem miss steps that the current query does not express, summaries drop exact strings, and pairing the two fixes the split of the budget in advance. We propose FlexA-Mem, a general memory that writes each unit of history once into an immutable store and renders a fresh memory for every call. The rendered memory is a compact timeline of records plus detail that a fixed rule fits into the remaining room without an LLM call. The detail is either relevant units as raw text or excerpts or the verbatim pieces that best match the query. With one store, FlexA-Mem serves both kinds of scenario. On AppWorld challenge tasks at 4k, it outperforms the second-best method by 11.5%, and on 147 unused tasks with predictions fixed in advance it outperforms A-Mem with a summary by 12.2%. On LongMemEval and LoCoMo, it matches a dedicated keyword retriever that writes no memory, while memories built on text written by an LLM fall far behind at tight budgets. Ablations show that the timeline carries AppWorld completion, whereas recovery mainly saves steps there and decides accuracy on exact facts. Code is available at https://github.com/WujiangXu/Flex-Amem

W7223890343.abstract: Disease diagnosis is a key application of large language model (LLM) agents in healthcare. However, existing medical agents are primarily trained and evaluated with static question-answering data, providing limited opportunities to learn active information acquisition, examination decision-making, and dynamic clinical interaction. To address this limitation, we present ClinVerse, an interactive, real-data-grounded multi-agent environment designed for training and evaluating medical diagnostic agents. Built on ClinPatient, a scalable dataset comprising 150k diagnostic cases derived from real-world electronic health records, ClinVerse supports coordinated interactions among six specialized clinical roles. Specifically, a doctor agent starts from an initial patient complaint, progressively gathers clinical evidence through patient interviews and examination requests, and ultimately produces a diagnosis. For each interaction trajectory, a rule-based scoring framework quantifies information acquisition, examination ordering, and diagnostic accuracy. These trajectory-level scores serve as reward signals for agent training while also enabling scalable evaluation. In experiments, we evaluate various general-purpose and medical-domain models and show that nine self-evolution methods across three categories consistently improve agents' diagnostic capabilities within ClinVerse. We further analyze the interplay among model capability, environment feedback, and self-evolution methods.

W7223892974.abstract: Autonomous mobile robot (AMR) fleets are increasingly used to move inventory inside warehouses, but the task-allocation logic that decides which robot serves which order is often either a fixed, non-adaptive dispatch rule or a proprietary black box. This paper reports a real, reproducible simulation study comparing three fully transparent, non-learned orchestration policies for a simulated autonomous ground vehicle (AGV) fleet performing pickup-and-delivery tasks in a warehouse grid: a static zone-assignment baseline, a reactive nearest-idle-agent heuristic, and a deterministic multi-signal market-auction mechanism that scores agents on travel distance, battery reserve, local congestion, and task-completion fairness. None of the three policies is a large language model or any other opaque learned controller; every decision rule is a plain, auditable function of observable state. Collision-free motion is guaranteed by Cooperative A* path planning over a shared space-time reservation table. We inject four real fault conditions (agent breakdown, aisle congestion, accelerated battery drain, and order-arrival surge) individually and in combination, and run 144 independent, seeded trials (three policies times six fault conditions times eight seeds, 1,200-tick horizon each) over a fixed 20x14-cell warehouse floor plan with four shelf blocks, three pack stations, and two charging stations. The market-auction policy and the reactive nearest-idle heuristic perform statistically indistinguishably on throughput and wait time under every fault condition (Welch's t-test, all p > 0.16), but the market-auction policy recovers from an injected agent breakdown in a mean of 14 simulation ticks versus 40 ticks for both other policies, a deterministic consequence of its shorter heartbeat-timeout window rather than a stochastic effect. The static zone-assignment baseline is significantly slower than both adaptive policies in every single condition, including with no faults injected at all (Welch's t-test, p < 0.001 for mean wait and cycle time in five of six conditions), and its completion rate collapses to roughly 90% under order-surge and combined-fault stress (chi-square test of independence, p < 0.001) while both adaptive policies sustain at or near 100% completion. We report these results, including the cases where the proposed market-auction policy shows no measurable advantage over the simpler reactive heuristic, as an honest, pilot-scale reference implementation rather than a claim of universal superiority, and we discuss the specific architectural property, heartbeat-timeout duration, responsible for the one place the two adaptive policies clearly diverge.

W7224123220.abstract: Abstract This paper investigates the application of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) to eigenvalue problems governed by partial differential equations, with the two-dimensional time-independent Schrödinger equation taken as a representative example. To address the limitations of traditional numerical methods in handling complex boundaries and high-dimensional problems, we propose a PINN framework in which the energy eigenvalue E is treated as a trainable parameter, together with a hybrid optimization strategy combining Adam and L-BFGS. To compute the ground state and multiple excited states simultaneously, normalization and orthogonality constraints between wave functions are incorporated into the loss function. Numerical experiments are conducted on several geometric domains, including circular, square, pentagram-shaped, and stadium-shaped boundaries. The results show that, for regular and symmetric domains, the PINN method achieves higher accuracy than the finite difference method in calculating low-energy levels. By using independent parameterization and orthogonality constraints, the method can effectively identify energy degeneracies caused by geometric symmetry. For irregular boundaries, the mesh-free nature of PINNs avoids the difficulty of complex mesh generation and demonstrates good adaptability and potential. Owing to its mesh-free formulation, ability to preserve geometric symmetry, and potential for extension to high-dimensional problems, the PINN method provides an effective and promising approach for solving eigenvalue problems with complex boundary conditions.

W7224178774.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) has become a key approach for large language model (LLM) compression.Existing methods commonly adopt block-level reconstruction as a surrogate to calibrate each quantized Transformer block.However, our analysis shows that this loose objective can admit cancellation patterns, where the aggregated block-level reconstruction error is small even though the per-head errors remain large.We therefore revisit the PTQ formulation from a variational perspective.By treating per-head representations as latent variables and the block output as the observed variable, we find that conventional block-level reconstruction corresponds to optimizing only the observation-level term, while omitting a latent alignment term that captures head-level quantization error.Motivated by this finding, we propose HEAL, a Latent HEad ALignment framework that turns block-level reconstruction calibration into joint observation-latent calibration with stop-gradient head alignment.Experiments on LLaMA-2/3 and Qwen2.5 families under low-bit weight-activation quantization show that HEAL generally improves perplexity and zero-shot accuracy over block-level reconstruction baselines.

W7224507277.abstract: This paper evaluates whether large language models (LLMs) can demonstrate cultural competence in Egyptian Arabic-not just factual knowledge about culture, but the ability to choose culturally appropriate idiomatic and figurative expressions in everyday social situations.67 Egyptian participants completed a multiple-choice questionnaire of 90 everyday scenarios to provide human gold labels.Using the same scenarios, each pairing a culturally appropriate Egyptian idiom against a plausible distractor, we evaluated 11 open-source and 3 proprietary models under five prompts and two answer orderings.The results indicated that humans performed near ceiling (98.2%), while LLMs averaged 68.2%.The results also showed that a single accuracy figure conflates three separable behaviors: cultural competence, an answer-position heuristic, and abstention.These behaviors are distributed so unevenly that the model ranking reorders depending on which one is measured.One model's apparent mid-tier accuracy is almost entirely a "pick the first option" heuristic (a 0.75 normal-reversed gap), and another falls from 51.8% to below chance once refusals to answer are scored as errors.We argue that cultural-competence evaluation should report this decomposition rather than a headline accuracy.

W7224762459.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged to be one of the most radical ideas in artificial intelligence since it enables the learner to learn the desired behavior through a response to the environment. The survey provides the overall picture of reinforcement learning, its development history beginning with the classical techniques up to the state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning algorithms. The paper provides a comprehensive explanation of the concepts and algorithmic structures and theoretical under-pinnings of the current RL systems. Such value-based approaches discussed in this paper include Q-Learning and Deep Q-Networks, such policy gradient techniques as REINFORCE and Actor-Critic, and such more sophisticated techniques as Trust Region Policy Optimization and Proximal Policy Optimization. This paper focuses on the more recent developments in model-based RL, multi-agent systems and hierarchical reinforcement learning and also offers commentary on the application to robotics, game playing, autonomous systems and resource management. Additionally, this methodology describes such issues as the efficiency of the sample, the conflict between exploration and exploitation, and safety issues and offers some of the prospects of future studies. As a source, it is not only an introduction to new readers, but also an independently useful resource to researchers who may wish to discover what the state of the field of reinforcement learning is.

W7224802209.abstract: The rapid growth in the size of state-of-the-art machine-learning (ML) models has led to increasing compute demands, spurring the development of energy-efficient hardware accelerators. Physical systems trained to perform ML inference, known as physical neural networks, have been proposed as accelerators in part because of their potential to be highly energy efficient. However, the ML inference accuracies reported in most investigations of physical neural networks have been substantially below the state of the art for conventional digital neural networks. In this work, we show in simulation studies that by applying modern ML training practices, including model compression, various candidate physical neural networks based on nonlinear dynamical systems can achieve accuracies as high as 99.2% on MNIST handwritten-digit recognition. We also show for one dynamical system that using it as the core building block of a parameter-efficient ML architecture inspired by MLP-Mixers enables accuracies of up to 86.4% on CIFAR-10 image classification (92.2% with pretraining and knowledge distillation), compared with 64% for the same system without the mixer architecture. The mixer approach achieved its accuracy while using $>5\times$ fewer trainable parameters than the baseline. Finally, we present back-of-the-envelope estimates for inference energy efficiency and speed when using an example physical dynamical system, suggesting that orders of magnitude improvements may be possible over digital-electronic neural networks.

W7224849782.abstract: Abstract Metal halide and lead-free double perovskites are promising materials for next-generation photovoltaics. But it is a challenge to navigate their huge compositional space and to simultaneously control long-term stability and non-radiative recombination. This review provides a critical synthesis of the cross-scale computational paradigm that brings together Density Functional Theory (DFT), machine learning (ML) and macroscopic device simulations like SCAPS-1D. We discuss how to transform first-principles atomistic parameters such as band edge alignments, dielectric constants and effective masses into meaningful device parameters without physical oversimplification. This work does not see parameter transfer as a "plug-and-play" process, but rather explains the bridging mechanisms that must be developed between microscopic energetics and macroscopic transport equations. We critically assess functional dependencies, active learning efficiencies, device-level limitations, and uncertainties related to ion migration and transient dynamics. This review provides actionable roadmap towards high-throughput physics-informed computational discovery of robust perovskite solar cells.

W7224901722.abstract: Effective multi-domain adaptation of large language models requires prioritizing relevant domain knowledge while minimizing interference from irrelevant domains. Existing approaches commonly use Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to train a separate adapter for each domain and combine these adapters within one model. However, they either weight adapters equally regardless of the input domain or dynamically weight adapters while still activating all of them including irrelevant ones. Additionally, while efficient, their low-rank structure limits performance. In contrast, upcycling is a model expansion method that adds experts and a router to a dense Transformer layer offering larger capacity than LoRA approaches. In this paper, we propose Domain-Specialized Upcycling (DS-Upcycling) for multi-domain adaptation. We introduce a new domain-aware supervision that allows the router to effectively learn to distinguish domains by selecting the appropriate experts. During fine-tuning on each new domain, we update only the corresponding expert and router while freezing all other parameters. Experiments show that our method achieves the highest average performance across the adapted domains compared to baselines while retaining general performance. With just 256 examples per domain for router supervision, DS-Upcycling achieves 90-98% routing accuracy after adaptation compared with 43-70% for routers trained without our approach.

W7224999084.abstract: To address the requirement for comprehensive analysis of multi-source geological information and intelligent decision-making in shale oil exploration and development, we propose a method for constructing a domain-specific large language model (LLM) for the shale oil, along with a framework for building and evaluating an LLM-based intelligent agent for shale oil seismic processing and interpretation. Using Qwen2.5-72B and Qwen3-32B as foundation models, we construct a specialized corpus of 21 billion tokens by integrating public shale oil literature and domain knowledge graphs. Leveraging expert annotation and model generation, we also construct 5.8×10 4 question-answer pairs in specific domain with high quality to serve as supervised fine-tuning dataset. We build a multi-stage efficient domain adaptation training framework for the shale oil large language model. First, domain knowledge is injected via task-aware continuous pre-training method, and supervised fine-tuning is executed using Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) combined with context-parallel algorithms. Then, direct preference optimization (DPO) and group relative strategy optimization (GRPO) are employed to align domain-specific preferences and enhance reasoning capabilities. In addition, a reflective retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework is built to optimize the accuracy and interpretability of model output. To enhance the tool-use capabilities of LLM and effectively mitigate hallucinations during tool-use process, we construct a specialized toolset by selecting open-source geoscience tools and employ targeted fine-tuning focused on tool utilization. Building on the foundation, we develop an intelligent scheduling service leveraging the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to deeply integrate core functions, such as seismic data processing, seismic interpretation, visualization, and report generation, thereby creating an LLM-driven agent for seismic processing and interpretation of shale oil. Experimental results demonstrate that the shale-oil domain-specific LLM achieves significantly higher accuracy in specialized Q&A compared to general-purpose foundation models, exhibiting excellent domain adaptability. Furthermore, following supervised fine-tuning using geoscience tools, the tool-use capability of shale-oil domain-specific LLM has been improved significantly compared with open-source foundation models.

W7225058323.abstract: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a new paradigm that allows intelligent systems to behave independently, pursue specific objectives, and adapt to changing circumstances. Agentic AI combines reasoning, planning, memory, learning, and tool utilization to do complicated tasks with minimal human involvement, in contrast to traditional AI systems that mainly react to user inputs. In this article, takes a look at Agentic AI from every angle: its theoretical underpinnings, technological supports, architectural blueprints, and real-world uses. Many models and frameworks are covered, including cognitive and modular designs, systems based on reinforcement learning, hybrid models, and multi-agent systems. Symbolic, probabilistic, and self-reflective reasoning are some of the reasoning methodologies covered. Classical, hierarchical, and adaptive planning strategies are also covered. Agents' ability to reliably and efficiently execute tasks is investigated by looking at memory management, communication protocols, coordination mechanisms, and collaborative decision-making. A wide range of business, medical, financial, academic, and personal aid apps are evaluated in the poll. Privacy, security, computational costs, scalability, and unexpected behavior are the main issues that are highlighted in the end. The study emphasizes the need for more investigation into how to create Agentic AI systems that are reliable, flexible, and effective.

W7225097661.abstract: Conventional crop breeding has delivered substantial yield and quality gains but faces persistent constraints from long breeding cycles, limited genetic diversity, and increasing climate volatility. Artificial intelligence (AI) and synthetic biology (SynBio) are emerging as complementary technologies that can accelerate allele discovery, trait design, and deployment across major staples and under-researched crops. Machine learning, computer vision, and robotics support high-throughput phenotyping from unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery and mobile devices, while genomic prediction models that integrate multi-omics and climate data can improve selection accuracy for traits such as yield stability and stress tolerance. SynBio platforms enable precise genome editing, synthetic circuits, and metabolic pathway engineering, with applications ranging from biofortified rice to multiplex editing in maize and pangenome-informed breeding in orphan crops such as chickpea and pearl millet. Their convergence, often described as “Breeding 5.0,” supports AI-guided design–build–test–learn (DBTL) cycles that optimize ideotypes for resource efficiency, resilience, and nutrition while reducing reliance on agrochemical inputs. This narrative review outlines the evolution from classical to molecular breeding, synthesizes current AI–SynBio pipelines with illustrative case studies, and highlights persistent challenges in data quality, transformation efficiency, biosafety, regulatory harmonization, and equitable access. We conclude with priorities for inclusive innovation to ensure that climate-smart, nutritious crops benefit diverse agroecosystems responsibly.

W7225111545.abstract: In oil and gas exploration and development, large language models and foundation models offer a new basis for integrating knowledge, data and engineering workflows. However, fragmented applications and unclear distinctions between model capabilities obscure how these technologies can support integrated decision-making. This review synthesizes the development and upstream applications of these models through a layered framework linking multimodal representation, domain knowledge, engineering computation, and operational decision-making. The findings indicate that the principal value of these models lies in connecting established petroleum technologies across disciplinary and organizational boundaries, rather than replacing specialized models or physical understanding. Within this framework, language models support knowledge interaction and workflow coordination, while foundation models extend representation learning across heterogeneous subsurface and operational data. The integration of these models with engineering models provides a pathway from isolated task automation toward coordinated intelligence across the exploration and development life cycle. The central challenge is to translate general model capabilities into reliable, transferable and economically sustainable engineering systems under geological uncertainty and operational constraints. However, addressing this task requires a closer integration of domain knowledge and physical mechanisms, alongside consistent data semantics and workflow-level evaluation. Herein, a staged development pathway is proposed, progressing from scenario-specific assistance to cross-disciplinary collaboration and bounded autonomous operation. This perspective reframes petroleum artificial intelligence as a system-integration problem and provides a conceptual basis for advancing human-machine collaboration in complex energy-resource development. W7225125113.abstract: Deploying large Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) and Large Language Models (LLMs) on resource-constrained hardware remains challenging due to their high computational, memory, and energy requirements. Conventional compression techniques, including pruning, quantization, and architectural optimization, can reduce these costs effectively; however, they often rely on manually designed heuristics and rule-based strategies. Such approaches face difficulties in efficiently exploring the large search spaces of modern neural architectures, frequently leading to sub-optimal trade-offs between model accuracy and efficiency. To address these limitations, Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as an effective framework for automated model compression by formulating the optimization process as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). Although numerous RL-based compression methods have recently been proposed, existing survey studies primarily categorize the literature according to the compression type, such as pruning or quantization, while providing limited analysis of the underlying RL mechanisms and design strategies. To address this gap, this survey presents, to the best of current knowledge, the first comprehensive RL-centric taxonomy for model compression. The state-of-the-art methods are systematically analyzed across four key dimensions: (1) MDP modeling strategies, including sequential layer-wise, topology-aware, multi-agent, dynamic runtime, and efficient environment modeling formulations; (2) action space design, covering quantization-oriented, pruning-oriented, joint compression, dynamic input-adaptive, and hierarchical action spaces; (3) reward function engineering, including accuracy-oriented, compression-aware, hardware-aware, multi-objective, and task-specific reward formulations; and (4) reinforcement learning algorithms, encompassing value-based methods, actor–critic approaches, policy-gradient techniques, Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), and hybrid/model-based RL frameworks. The survey further examines recent developments ranging from pruning and mixed-precision quantization in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to token pruning, context compression, and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) pruning in Vision Transformers (ViTs) and LLMs, highlighting the relationships between RL design choices and compression performance. The review also describes the literature-selection scope, summarizes representative quantitative results, and discusses key limitations affecting scalability, transferability, benchmarking, and deployment. Overall, this paper provides a structured RL-centric perspective on automated model compression, identifies current challenges and research gaps, and outlines promising directions for developing scalable, adaptive, and hardware-aware compression systems.

W7225164364.abstract: The term agentic AI is now applied to systems that range from a chatbot permitted to call a calculator to a persistent, self-directing orchestrator that spawns sub-agents, browses the open web and executes irreversible actions in production environments. Treating these as a single category obscures the fact that each step along that range introduces a distinct failure mode and a distinct accountability question. This paper proposes a taxonomy that makes the steps explicit. Drawing on the recent survey literature on language-model agents, on empirical work on tool-use and function-calling reliability, on the security literature on prompt injection in tool-integrated systems, and on the philosophical and legal literature on delegation, responsibility gaps and meaningful human control, it defines six levels of autonomy for tool-using language-model agents (responder, tool-calling assistant, bounded executor, goal-directed agent, orchestrating agent and persistent autonomous agent) and three cross-cutting dimensions along which any agent at any level can be positioned: the action surface it can reach, the environment it is exposed to, and the oversight regime under which it runs. For each level the paper identifies the characteristic failure modes and the accountability instruments that remain feasible. Its central argument is that accountability does not diminish as autonomy rises, as the delegation framing implies, but must be deliberately scaled up with it, and that most current deployments invert this relationship by expanding autonomy faster than they expand the instruments by which a human can answer for what the agent does. The paper closes with seven design principles for bounded autonomy, a note on deployment under infrastructure constraints, and a research agenda.

W7225231650.abstract: We propose a physics-informed neural network (PINN) approach for high-fidelity quantum gate learning in both one- and two-qubit systems. We train a PINN using the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, where smooth control fields with fixed boundary conditions are obtained by minimizing a loss function that considers model dynamics, gate error, physical constraints, regularization terms, and multiple initial conditions. Training considers pairs of mutually unbiased bases, while independent validation combines Haar-random input states with the average gate fidelity. Unitary simulations yield an average gate infidelity of $8.49\times10^{-8}$ for Hadamard and values between $3.39\times10^{-7}$ and $4.96\times10^{-6}$ for controlled-NOT under $XX$, $YY$, and $ZZ$ interactions. We examine how the learned control fields depend on the coupling, training configuration, and available local fields, including five exchange-type dipolar scenarios. We test the learned control fields under the Lindblad master equation with dephasing and amplitude damping, theoretically reproducing the expected first-order fidelity loss in the weak-dissipation regime. Finally, boundary-adapted Chebyshev expansions represent 139 learned controls with a minimum common count of $K_\ast=24$ coefficients per control for all eleven family-averaged mean squared errors to fall below $10^{-6}$. Separately, square-pulse and Strang propagation at $K=30$ preserve all 31 continuous polynomial references within infidelity $10^{-5}$ at $N=128$ and all larger tested resolutions, under both sampling rules. These results connect multi-state gate synthesis, control-resource characterization, and compact square-pulse playback.

W7225246242.abstract: We solve five equations from quantum cosmology, gauge theory, relativistic quantum mechanics and random matrix theory with physics-informed neural networks trained entirely on a single CPU, and we do it without a deep-learning framework. The objectives are supplied by optimiz-rs, a Rust optimisation library; the automatic differentiation is thotgrad, a 261-line reverse-mode tape over NumPy written for this study; the optimisers are thotopt, a 130-line AdamW and L-BFGS pair. The methodological point is a composition rule which lets an objective defined outside the differentiation tape contribute an exact gradient through a single vector–Jacobian product. This separates the definition of a loss from the machinery that differentiates it, so one audited implementation of cross-entropy or weighted mean-squared error serves every model in a stack, and we show that the arrangement costs nothing in accuracy: the assembled gradient agrees with central finite differences to 4×10⁻⁸ relative error. For each equation we give the derivation, state existence and uniqueness precisely, and validate the trained network against an independent reference rather than against itself — Numerov integration for Wheeler–DeWitt, spectral inversion of the periodic Laplacian for Hermitian Yang–Mills, the exactly diagonalised propagator for Dirac, and the simulated particle system together with the analytic semicircle transform for McKean–Vlasov. Relative errors range from 2.4×10⁻⁴ to 9.8×10⁻², and total training time for all four networks is 213 seconds on one Intel i9-8950HK. We give the cost model in closed form — Θ((1+2d)NLW²) per loss-and-gradient for d inputs, N collocation points and L layers of width W — and use it to say where the no-accelerator choice stops being the right one, which is when the working set leaves last-level cache rather than when the parameter count grows. Two diagnostics were deliberately excluded from the objectives so that they constitute evidence rather than assumption: unitarity of the Dirac evolution, which is never imposed and holds to 10⁻³, and Wigner's semicircle law, which the McKean–Vlasov network recovers having been given only a complex Burgers equation and an initial condition. We also report, with reproducible evidence, two solver defects the validation protocol caught in our own library. The complete reproduction artifact — notebook, tape, optimisers, problem definitions and a 25-check finite-difference test suite — is deposited with the paper and runs end to end on one CPU in four minutes.
